This slice builds the handshake and everything that guards it — the stateless cookie, the amplification bound, version and capacity refusals, session identity and demultiplexing. It does not yet carry data; the packet records, the four sequence Spaces, fragmentation and the acknowledgement machinery land in the slices that follow, and SessionEventKind grows with them. public sealed class DatagramSessionReactor : IDisposable Inheritance object DatagramSessionReactor Implements IDisposable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Endpoints are declared, not registered. Unlike RawReactor, which hands back a LinkId for every socket a consumer registers, this Reactor takes its endpoints on Endpoints at construction and never rebinds (ADR 0014). Binding returns no identity because there is nothing to address: a consumer addresses Peers, and a Peer is not a socket. A Reactor that declares no endpoints binds nothing until its first Connect(IPEndPoint), which binds one wildcard, port-zero socket in the destination's address family and appends it to BoundEndpoints. Capacity counts Peers. The bound sockets are not share-holders and hold no read share (ADR 0014): a Peer's Messages arrive through whichever socket happens to carry them, so charging the arena per socket would give one Peer on a single-socket Reactor the whole arena and sixty-four Peers a sixty-fourth each — exactly inverted. The read share is the arena divided by Capacity, and it belongs to the Peer. What a stranger can make this Reactor do. Very little, and that is the design. Anything an unauthenticated remote can generate at will goes to the Diagnostic Sink and never to the event stream, so a stranger cannot write into the consumer's protocol. Every reply to an unverified sender is exactly one control datagram of ReactorSockets.Session.DatagramSessionProtocol.ControlDatagramSize bytes, answering exactly one control datagram of the same size, so bytes sent never exceed bytes received and this Reactor cannot be used to amplify a flood at a spoofed third party. A bare Hello is answered with a Cookie whatever it claimed — never a Refusal — so nothing about this Reactor's version or occupancy is learnable without first proving the ability to receive at the address claimed. The wire session id is not an authenticator. It is a receiver-assigned random 32-bit demultiplexing token: unguessable enough that an off-path attacker cannot address a Session it was never introduced to, and nothing more. This library does not encrypt, does not authenticate the data plane, and an on-path attacker who can read a datagram can forge one. Consumers needing confidentiality or integrity must layer it themselves. ReactorSockets.DiagnosticId.html.title: Enum DiagnosticId | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DiagnosticId.html.summary: Enum DiagnosticId Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll A closed, permanent enumeration of diagnostic causes with explicit values in reserved blocks — common 1-99, Raw 100-199, datagram session 200-299, stream session 300-399 (ADR 0013) — so a future insertion cannot silently renumber an id a consumer has persisted. There is no None or Unknown member and zero is never used: every DiagnosticRecord has a cause by construction. public enum DiagnosticId Fields AdmissionCapReached = 1 The configured admission cap was hit this Pump with work still waiting to be admitted. No subject. Value0 is the cap, Value1 is the count of Admissions declined, counted as the Reactor's counters count them: once per declining where the work waits out of reach — a listening Link or bound endpoint with a pending connection it left in the OS backlog, never the number of connections left there, a depth unknowable without accepting — and once per piece of work where the Reactor was holding it, whether it then waits or is Discarded. ArenaExhausted = 2 The frame arena had no room left for a request, regardless of the read-share escape. Subject is the Link that made the request. Value0 is the bytes requested, Value1 is the arena's bytes free at the moment of the request. CapacityExhausted = 3 Every capacity slot was occupied this Pump with work still waiting to be admitted — a different exhaustion from AdmissionCapReached, reachable because the admission cap can be configured above Capacity. No subject. Value0 is the capacity, Value1 is the count of Admissions declined, counted the same way and with the same limit as AdmissionCapReached's. LinkFailed = 100 A registered Link failed and closed. Subject is the Link. Value0 carries the platform SocketError as its underlying integer value; Value1 is unused. DestinationUnreachable = 101 An ICMP port-unreachable (or platform equivalent) was reported for a send. Subject is the Link. Value0 carries the platform SocketError as its underlying integer value; Value1 is unused. DatagramTruncated = 102 A datagram exceeded the Reactor's scratch buffer and was truncated. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the scratch buffer size in bytes; Value1 is unused. DatagramMalformed = 200 A datagram was discarded because nothing in it could be attributed to a Peer: wrong length, an unknown control type, a body the declared type cannot fill, padding that was not zero, a session id naming no Session, or a well-formed control reply — a Cookie, an Accept, a Refusal — matching no dial this Reactor is waiting on. That last case is not a parse failure, but it is the same thing to a consumer: bytes arrived, named nobody, and went nowhere. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the bytes received; Value1 is unused. A remote can produce this at will by sending rubbish, which is exactly why it is a Diagnostic and never an Event: the event stream is the consumer's protocol, and an unauthenticated stranger must not be able to write to it. Warn rather than Error for the same reason — nothing is wrong with this Reactor. CookieRejected = 201 A Hello carried a cookie this Reactor did not mint, or minted too long ago: a forged or corrupted authenticator, a cookie replayed from a different source address, or one from an epoch older than the previous. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the epoch the cookie offered; Value1 is the epoch current at the moment it was checked. Warn, never Error: a cookie arriving one epoch after it was minted is the mechanism working, and a Reactor visible to the internet will see forged ones continuously. Raising this to Error would train a consumer to ignore Error. VersionRefused = 202 A cookie-validated Hello offered a protocol version this Reactor does not speak, and was refused. Subject is the claimed Source. Value0 is the version offered; Value1 is the version this Reactor requires. Emitted only for a Hello that passed the cookie check, because that is the only Hello a Reactor answers at all — a bare Hello is answered with a Cookie and nothing else, whatever version it claimed. PeerRefused = 300 A dialler was refused in-protocol during the stream handshake, either because it announced a different protocol version or because every capacity Slot was occupied. Subject is the claimed Source: at refusal time there is no Peer, only a claimed origin. For a capacity refusal, Value0 is this Reactor's capacity and Value1 is unused. For a version refusal, Value0 is the version offered and Value1 is the version this Reactor requires. Info, not Warn: a version mismatch on an upgrade and an ordinary burst at capacity are both routine, expected outcomes of running this profile, not conditions a consumer needs to act on. LingerNegotiated = 301 A stream handshake completed and the two ends' announced Linger values were negotiated to their minimum (ADR 0011). Subject is the newly established Peer. Value0 is this end's own Linger in milliseconds; Value1 is the effective (minimum) Linger in milliseconds. MalformedFraming = 302 An established Peer's Message framing broke this profile's rules and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation: an oversized or zero-length prefix, or a stream that ended before a prefix or the Message body it named had fully arrived. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the offending length prefix — 0 for a truncation, where no full prefix was ever read; Value1 is this Reactor's own MaxMessageSize. Warn: a remote can produce this at will by sending malformed bytes, which is exactly why the Session ends rather than throws, and why this is a Diagnostic rather than an Event on the consumer's own stream. DataAfterGoodbye = 303 An established Peer sent Message bytes after its own Goodbye had already been received, and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation (issue #93). Subject is the Peer. Carries no claimed length — ReactorSockets.Session.MessageFramingLegality reaches this outcome before ever reading a prefix, so there is nothing to report but the contradiction itself. Value0 and Value1 are unused. Warn, for the same reason as MalformedFraming: a remote can produce this at will by ignoring the Goodbye it just sent. ResumeMatched = 304 A connection presenting a valid resume secret was matched onto the Interrupted Peer whose Slot was reserving the Session it named, and that Session continued over the replacement transport rather than a new one being established (issue #123, ADR 0011). Subject is the resumed Peer — the same PeerId, generation included, the Session had before the interruption, since nothing about a Peer's identity is renewed by a Resume. Value0 is the number of retained outbound bytes the match rewound to the counter the Resume reported; Value1 is unused. Info: a reconnection is the outcome reserving a Slot exists to produce, not a condition a consumer needs to act on. Value0 reads 0 until issue #127 supplies the rewind: this slice matches the Resume and reads the counter it reports without acting on it, so no bytes have been rewound yet and 0 is what the match can honestly report. Numbered 304 rather than the 302 the slice-4 spec named: 302 and 303 were taken by MalformedFraming and DataAfterGoodbye (issues #92 and #106) after that spec was written, and a value published in a closed permanent enum is never renumbered. ResumeUnmatched = 305 A connection claiming an existing Session was refused rather than resumed. Subject is the claimed Source: a claim that is not matched comes from a party that is by construction not a Peer, so there is no Peer to name, only a claimed origin. Value0 is the number of Interrupted Peers whose reservations the claim was checked against — 0 means nothing was being held at all, which is the reconfiguration path where a once-valid secret arrives after its Linger expired. Value1 is the wire record type the claim arrived as: 3 for a Resume whose secret matched no held Peer, and 1 for a Hello presenting a secret that did match, which re-announces the parameters a Resume has no field for and is refused as a protocol violation. Warn rather than the Info a version mismatch or a capacity refusal carries: those are routine outcomes of running this profile and a wrong secret is not. "Unmatched" names the outcome, not the comparison: the claim was not matched onto a Session. The Hello case reaches here having found the secret it announced, and is refused anyway because the record it arrived in re-announces parameters — Value1 is what tells the two apart. Value0 is reported to this end's own Sink and never to the wire: a refused party is closed on without being told anything, so it learns neither the count nor which of the three refusals it met. RedialAttempted = 306 A dialling-side Peer began a fresh re-dial attempt after its transport was lost (issue #125, ADR 0011). Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the attempt number, starting at 1 and rising by one per attempt; Value1 is the delay in milliseconds this attempt actually waited before dialling — the jittered figure ReactorSockets.Session.RedialSchedule.NextDelay() drew, so what actually elapsed is observable rather than only the computed figure before jitter. Info: a re-dial is the ordinary behaviour of a dialling Peer that lost its transport, not a condition a consumer needs to act on. RedialFailed = 307 A re-dial attempt could not connect (issue #125, ADR 0011). Subject is the Peer, which this never closes — it stays Interrupted and waits out the schedule's next delay, leaving Linger, not an attempt count, the only thing that ever closes it. Value0 carries the platform SocketError as its underlying integer value; Value1 is the attempt number that failed. Info rather than Warn: under this profile's premise a failed reconnection attempt is an ordinary, expected outcome, and raising it to Warn would train a consumer to ignore Warn. DeliveryCounterRefused = 308 An established Peer's delivery-counter record (issue #109) claimed to have received more Messages than this end has ever sent it, and the Session was closed with ProtocolViolation (issue #113) — the peer is confirming Messages this end never queued, rather than merely repeating a count it already reported. Subject is the Peer. Value0 is the claimed cumulative count; Value1 is the count of Messages (and, if this end's own Goodbye has already been queued for this Peer, that too) this end has actually appended to this Peer's retention — the largest count a legitimate confirmation could ever sit at or below. Warn, for the same reason as MalformedFraming: a remote can produce this at will by inflating its own counter. Numbered 308 rather than the next free 304: ADR 0013's roster, as amended for this slice, reserves 304-307 for the rest of slice 4 (ResumeMatched and ResumeUnmatched, which issue #124 has since taken, then RedialAttempted and RedialFailed), and a value published in a closed permanent enum cannot be moved later to make room.

ReactorSockets.DisconnectReason.html.title: Enum DisconnectReason | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.DisconnectReason.html.summary: Enum DisconnectReason Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Why a Peer's Session ended, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration. Deliberately not shared with the Raw profile's CloseReason (ADR 0008): most of the members a Session needs are protocol vocabulary Raw can never produce, and a single shared enumeration would leave one profile documenting members it cannot emit. public enum DisconnectReason Fields LocalClose = 0 The consumer called Close on this Peer. VersionMismatch = 1 The two ends do not speak the same protocol version. The version match is exact — there is no negotiation, no lowest-common-version rule and no compatibility range — so this is produced both by the end that refused and by the end whose Hello was refused. RemoteAtCapacity = 2 The remote end had no capacity Slot free for this Session and said so. Distinct from silence: a Reactor at capacity answers a Hello it received rather than dropping it, so the dialler learns the difference between "full" and "gone". TransportFailed = 3 The underlying transport failed or ended before or during the handshake: a reset, a dial that could not connect, or a stream that closed before a full handshake record arrived. Distinct from every other member here because nothing about the protocol was at fault — the byte stream itself did not survive to carry it. Since issue #119, the same kind of failure on an established Peer no longer produces this reason at all — it moves the Peer to PeerInterrupted instead, because its identity and undelivered Messages are still worth holding for a Resume. This member now fires only for a Peer that never finished becoming one. ProtocolViolation = 4 An established Peer's Message framing broke this profile's rules: a length prefix exceeding the announced MaxMessageSize, a length prefix of zero, a stream that ended before a length prefix or the Message body it named had fully arrived, or bytes arriving behind a Goodbye already received from that Peer (issue #93) — a Peer that announced it was leaving and then kept sending is contradicting its own announcement, so it is disconnected rather than believed. Distinct from TransportFailed: the byte stream itself survived long enough to carry the violation, and what is wrong is the bytes it carried rather than the transport underneath it. Distinct from PeerGoodbye, which is reserved for an ending that stayed clean to the last byte. PeerGoodbye = 5 The remote Peer sent a Goodbye: it is ending the Session on purpose rather than failing (issue #23). Produced once whatever this end still held for it has finished flushing — immediately, if nothing was outstanding when the Goodbye arrived, or after the Closing Session it entered (PeerClosing) has drained. LingerExpired = 6 An PeerInterrupted Peer's effective Linger — the value LingerNegotiated already reported at handshake (ADR 0011), the minimum of the two ends' announced Lingers — elapsed before the transport came back (issue #121). Linger, not the loss of the transport, is what closes an Interrupted Peer: the loss itself only produced PeerInterrupted (issue #119) and held the Peer's identity, counters and undelivered Messages open for a Resume. This member fires once that wait has run out, and is also what bounds a Close(PeerId) whose Goodbye can never reach a wire that no longer exists — without it, that Peer's retention would sit pending forever (issue #92). Distinct from TransportFailed, which means the byte stream never survived long enough to say anything at all — this means it survived, said nothing further within the time this end had promised to wait, and this end gave up on its own clock rather than being told to. Distinct from PeerGoodbye, which is an ending the remote announced on purpose while its transport still worked — this is an ending this end declares unilaterally, after silence, with no announcement possible because the transport that would have carried one is already gone. RetentionGap = 7 A Resume's reported delivery counter named a Message position below this end's retention ring — the peer confirmed nothing further, but by the time it reconnected the bytes at its reported position had already been released to make room for newer ones (RetentionExhausted during the interruption, issue #120). Resuming anyway would deliver a stream with a hole in it, so this end closes instead (issue #130). Distinct from LingerExpired and TransportFailed because both of those are silent about why the Session ended — nothing was wrong with what either side said, only with how long the transport stayed reachable — while this one is a direct statement about what the peer said: its retention window was too small for the outage it just had. That makes the remedy actionable and specific — raise this end's retention capacity or its Linger, or both — in a way neither of those two members is. The mirror case, a Resume counter naming a Message this end never sent at all, is not this member: that is a protocol violation (ProtocolViolation), not a capacity question, because no amount of retention would have made a fabricated counter valid. Remarks Explicit values throughout, house style since RawLinkLegality (PR #70): a member is added at the end with the next free number, never inserted, so a value a consumer has already persisted keeps its meaning across a library upgrade. Every place this library maps something else onto a DisconnectReason — a wire ReactorSockets.Session.RefusalReason, a malformed-framing outcome, a Goodbye control record — states that mapping as its own table with a discard arm that refuses rather than permits, the same house rule RawLinkLegality follows: an input this library does not recognise fails closed instead of being guessed at.

ReactorSockets.PeerCounters.-ctor.html.summary: Constructor PeerCounters Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll PeerCounters(ulong, ulong, ulong) A point-in-time snapshot of one Peer's counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from that Peer's establishment, with no reset, fetched by value and keyed by PeerId — mirrors LinkCounters's Raw-profile shape and the same "no accessor enumerates every Peer's counters in one call" rule. public PeerCounters(ulong MessagesReceived, ulong RetentionHighWaterBytes, ulong Resumes) Parameters MessagesReceived ulong Whole Messages handed to the frame arena for delivery — incremented at that point only, never when a Message's bytes finish arriving or while it sits buffered waiting for a read share or arena room (subtask 3.4.4, issue #82). This is what makes a share exhaustion visible: a Frame in which bytes plainly arrived but this figure did not move is a Message still buffered, not one dropped. RetentionHighWaterBytes ulong The most bytes this Peer's retention ring has ever held at once (written minus released) since the Peer was established — HighWaterBytes(int) read fresh at snapshot time, never pushed. Monotonic for the Peer's lifetime: draining the ring after a burst lowers what is currently retained but never lowers this figure (subtask 3.5.5, issue #87). Resumes ulong How many times this Peer's transport has been successfully resumed after an Interruption (issue #128, ADR 0013). Incremented once per PeerResumed raised for this Peer, on both the listening and dialling sides, and never on a refused resume. Earns its own member rather than being derived by the consumer counting PeerResumed Events: a Session profile drains Events into whatever cadence the consumer chooses, so counting them back out is not generally possible once drained, while this figure is a Counter — read fresh by value at any time, the same as every other figure here. Monotonic and never reset: a resume carries no counter's history away with it, so a retransmission count spanning several resumes is how a flapping path shows itself instead of being hidden by a zeroing on every reconnect.

ReactorSockets.PeerId.-ctor.html.title: Constructor PeerId | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.PeerId.-ctor.html.summary: Constructor PeerId Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll PeerId(ulong, int, ulong) A Peer's identity inside this process: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based Slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the Slot is reused, so a stale PeerId held past a Peer's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that Slot (ADR 0007) rather than aliasing it. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010), exactly as LinkId is the Raw profile's. public PeerId(ulong Origin, int Index, ulong Generation) Parameters Origin ulong Which Reactor issued this PeerId. Opaque and process-local — it is compared for equality and nothing else, orders nothing, and never appears on the wire. Not a Source, which names a remote address; this names a Reactor of this process. Index int The zero-based Slot this Peer occupies. Generation ulong The generation that Slot was on when this Peer was admitted. Live Slots begin at 1, so a default PeerId — generation 0 — addresses nothing. Remarks This is deliberately not the identity a datagram Session puts on the wire. A Slot index is dense, small and guessable, and a remote that can guess one can address a Peer it was never introduced to; the wire identity is instead a receiver-assigned random 32-bit value the two ends exchange during the handshake, and it never appears on this type. The generation is ulong rather than int so that it cannot wrap within the life of any process, which is what lets generation 0 stay a reserved sentinel without a check guarding it (ADR 0015). The Origin is what makes a PeerId mean something to exactly one Reactor. Without it, index and generation are only unique within a single Reactor's table, and every table's first Peer is Slot 0 generation 1 — so one Reactor's PeerId passed to another's Close named a live Peer of that second Reactor and closed it. A consumer running two Reactors gets the mistake back as nothing happening, which is what an id addressing no Peer has always meant here.

ReactorSockets.PumpIntervalObserver.html.summary: Class PumpIntervalObserver Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Measures the interval between consecutive Pump() calls from monotonic TimeProvider timestamps. This is what makes the re-dial schedule's initial delay (ReactorSockets.Session.RedialSchedule) derived rather than invented: a retry sooner than the next Pump cannot happen, so the next Pump is the floor, and the only way to know that floor is to watch how often Pump is actually called. public sealed class PumpIntervalObserver Inheritance object PumpIntervalObserver Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Public for the same reason ReactorSockets.Session.RedialSchedule is (ADR 0015): a test pins this behaviour by constructing one directly against a substituted TimeProvider and calling Observe() the same way a Reactor's own Pump would, with no InternalsVisibleTo and no interface invented for the purpose. Link, Source and Payload are populated. Closed = 1 A Link closed. Link and Reason are populated. Accepted = 2 A connection was accepted on a listening Link, inside the Pump that found it ready. ListeningLink names the listening Link that fired; Link names the new connection, already registered and consuming a capacity slot of its own. Connected = 3 An outbound dial completed successfully, inside the Pump that found the connecting socket writable. Link is populated; a dial that fails instead produces Closed with Refused or Unreachable. SegmentReceived = 4 A run of bytes arrived on a stream Link. Link and Payload are populated. Carries no claim of being a whole anything — a counterparty's single write may be drained as one or several of these, and framing is the consumer's decision, not this library's. EndOfStream = 5 The remote end of a stream Link will send nothing further while this Link remains open for sending — TCP's own half-close, kept separate from Closed because collapsing them would decide on the consumer's behalf that their protocol cannot use half-close. Link is populated. A consumer that never calls Close after this holds the Link and its slot until the Reactor is disposed — there is no Linger in Raw to reclaim it. Writable = 6 A stream Link that took fewer bytes than offered on a previous Send has become writable again. Link is populated. ReactorSockets.RawReactor.Send.html.summary: Method Send Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Send(LinkId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) Send is stream-only and illegal on a datagram or listening Link. Takes what the socket will accept of payload right now and reports the count — never blocks, never copies and never queues (ADR 0008): whatever the socket did not take stays with the caller, who decides whether and when to offer it again. Either way the Reactor would be inventing a per-Link FIFO policy, which is machinery a Session has and Raw was said not to lend. public SendResult Send(LinkId link, ReadOnlySpan<byte> payload) Parameters link LinkId payload ReadOnlySpan<byte> Returns SendResult Remarks A send that takes fewer bytes than payload.Length arms exactly one Writable for link: the next Pump() that finds the socket writable queues it and clears the mark, so a consumer using this Link only ever sees one Writable per short send, never one for every Pump a socket happens to be writable (nearly always). A Link never over-sent on produces no Writable at all — the event is a reply to something the consumer did, not a status this Reactor volunteers. When that one event arrives is the platform's call, not this Reactor's, and the platforms differ by more than a rounding error: Windows offers writability again as soon as the send buffer has any room, while Linux waits until roughly half of it is free. A Link whose counterparty reads slowly can therefore stay unwritable on Linux long after it would have been writable on Windows, with a large auto-tuned send buffer widening the gap. ReactorSockets.ReactorCounters.-ctor.htm.summary: Constructor ReactorCounters Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll ReactorCounters(ulong, ulong, ulong, ulong, ulong, ulong, ulong) A point-in-time snapshot of the Reactor-scope counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from construction, with no reset. Fetched by value so nothing lets a consumer hold a pointer into live state across a Pump; diffing two snapshots gives everything a reset would, from state the consumer already owns. public ReactorCounters(ulong SinkFaulted, ulong DatagramsSent, ulong DatagramsReceived, ulong ArenaHighWaterBytes, ulong AdmissionDeferrals, ulong AdmissionDiscards, ulong UnknownSourceDiscards) Parameters SinkFaulted ulong Times the installed Sink threw and was disabled for the Reactor's life. DatagramsSent ulong Datagrams handed to the transport for sending. DatagramsReceived ulong Datagrams taken from the transport. ArenaHighWaterBytes ulong The most Arena bytes any single Frame has used. AdmissionDeferrals ulong Admissions declined that left the work where it was, for a later Pump to take. Moves on the transports where declined work waits — Raw and the stream Session profile. Counted once per declining rather than once per piece of work turned away, which makes it coarse where the work sits in an OS backlog: one listening Link or bound endpoint declines its whole backlog with one declining, because that depth is unknowable without accepting. Where the Reactor already holds the work — a stream Session handshake accepted but not completed — one declining is one piece of work and the figure is exact. Read the magnitude as "how much of the listening fleet is turning work away", never as backlog depth. AdmissionDiscards ulong Admissions declined that let the work go, because the transport gave it nowhere to wait. Moves only on the datagram Session profile, which Discards the Hellos it cannot admit. Always an exact count of work turned away, which AdmissionDeferrals is not, because a Reactor can only Discard what it had in hand. Kept apart from Deferrals because the two differ in the one way a consumer would act on: deferred work arrives on a later Pump, Discarded work never does. UnknownSourceDiscards ulong Datagrams taken from the transport and thrown away because nothing could be attributed to a Peer: a malformed control datagram, or a session id naming no Session. Reactor-scope rather than per-Peer precisely because there is no Peer to charge them to — the whole point of the member is the traffic that failed to name one. Moves only on the datagram Session profile. A rising figure on a Reactor that is otherwise healthy is a scan or a flood, not a fault, which is why the matching Diagnostics are Warn. Remarks The shape is shared by every profile; which members move is not. DatagramsSent and DatagramsReceived stay at zero on a Reactor carrying no datagram transport, and the two admission counters divide the same way. A member that never moves on a profile is reporting a true zero, not a gap.

ReactorSockets.SessionEventKind.html.title: Enum SessionEventKind | ReactorSockets API reference
ReactorSockets.SessionEventKind.html.summary: Enum SessionEventKind Namespace ReactorSockets Assembly ReactorSockets.dll Which kind of SessionEvent was drained, and therefore which of its fields carry meaning. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010). public enum SessionEventKind Fields PeerConnected = 1 A Session is established and the Peer is addressable. Raised on both ends: on the dialler when the Accept arrives, on the accepting end when a Hello is admitted. PeerClosed = 2 A Session ended, or a dial never became one. Reason says why, and the PeerId is dead from this event onwards. MessageReceived = 3 A whole Message was reassembled from the Peer's stream and copied into the frame arena. Payload carries it, valid only until the next Pump (ADR 0008). PeerClosing = 4 The Peer's Goodbye arrived while something was still outstanding to deliver: either Messages this end had already reassembled from it but the consumer had not yet drained (issue #23 review finding — a Message queued ahead of the Goodbye in the same read counts, even though it reached MessageReceived first), or bytes still buffered in its receive share awaiting arena room (#81), or this end's own outbound retention for it still being flushed to the socket. The Peer accepts no further Sends worth making from here (issue #23) and a PeerClosed carrying PeerGoodbye follows once all of that is exhausted. Never raised when nothing was outstanding on either side — a Goodbye that finds the Peer already caught up closes it directly, with no zero-Frame Closing observable in between. PeerInterrupted = 5 The stream profile's transport for this Peer is gone, but the Peer itself is not: its PeerId — including generation — stays live, CountersOf(PeerId) keeps answering for it, and its undelivered inbound Messages and outbound retention ring are held rather than discarded (issue #119, ADR 0010). Raised whenever an established Peer's transport ends without a Goodbye first: an inbound FIN carrying nothing further, a reset, a local write failure, or this end's own receive-idle deadline expiring (revising issue #117, which closed the Peer outright before this kind existed). Distinct from PeerClosing: Closing means a Goodbye arrived and the Session is ending on purpose, with PeerClosed to follow once both sides drain — nothing here is ever resumable. Interrupted means the opposite — no Goodbye was ever seen, the Session is not ending, and the Peer sits ready for a Resume (a later slice) for as long as Linger allows (issue #121). A Peer that sent Goodbye and then a bare FIN reaches PeerClosing or PeerClosed, never this. Carries only Peer — there is no DisconnectReason to report, because nothing has ended. PeerResumed = 6 A Session held PeerInterrupted reclaimed its transport and is delivering again (issue #128, closing out #30's Resume). Raised on whichever side completes the match, and in both cases only once that side knows where to resend from: on the listening side from ResumeHeldPeer, once the peer's Resume record checks out and its carried delivery counter has driven the rewind; on the dialling side not from ResumeDialledPeer, which only sends the Resume record, but later, when the listening side's reciprocal delivery-counter record arrives and is rewound off (issue #127). Only that success path reaches here: a resume refused because the peer named a Message this end no longer retains closes the Peer instead (RetentionGap, issue #130) and never raises this. Peer's PeerId, generation included, is exactly the one PeerInterrupted carried — a Resume is the same Peer's transport coming back, never a new one — and no PeerClosed is ever observed between the two. The consumer is asked for no reconciliation: Messages sent before the interruption arrive without being re-sent, since the rewind that makes this event possible (issue #127) already put this end's outbound retention back to the peer's last confirmed point before this event is raised. Carries only Peer, the same as PeerInterrupted — nothing has ended, so there is no DisconnectReason to report. Remarks The roster grows with Resume across later slices. Members are appended, never inserted.

It does not yet carry data; the packet records, the four sequence Spaces, fragmentation and the acknowledgement machinery land in the slices that follow, and SessionEventKind grows with them. PumpIntervalObserver Measures the interval between consecutive Pump() calls from monotonic TimeProvider timestamps. This is what makes the re-dial schedule's initial delay (ReactorSockets.Session.RedialSchedule) derived rather than invented: a retry sooner than the next Pump cannot happen, so the next Pump is the floor, and the only way to know that floor is to watch how often Pump is actually called. RawReactor The escape hatch (ADR 0007): a consumer registers UDP sockets at runtime, gets a LinkId back for each, and advances everything with a single synchronous Pump() call from their own loop. Nothing is delivered except in response to a call the consumer made, on the thread that constructed this Reactor. TCP joins the datagram surface here: a listening Link and the connections it accepts are registered and admitted the same way, and a stream Link's reads drain as SegmentReceived and EndOfStream exactly like a datagram Link's. A stream Link's Send(LinkId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) takes what the socket will take and reports the count, arming exactly one Writable when it took fewer bytes than offered; Shutdown(LinkId) sends this Link's own FIN while it stays open for reading. ReactorOptions The budget L0 spends inside a Pump, shared by every profile. Composed as a member into each profile's options type rather than inherited from a base (ADR 0012) — nothing protocol-specific may ever enter this type, since a knob two of three profiles need is exactly what would turn it into the base class ADR 0011 refused. StreamSessionOptions The construction surface of a StreamSessionReactor (ADR 0011): the shared L0 budget composed in as Reactor, plus the knobs this profile alone has. Composed rather than inherited, so that nothing protocol-specific here can ever leak into ReactorOptions and turn it into the base class ADR 0011 refused. StreamSessionReactor The stream Session profile (ADR 0010): Sessions established over TCP, addressed as Peers, delivering u32 length-prefixed Messages rather than the byte runs the transport gives. Slices 3.1-3.3 validate StreamSessionOptions and its allocation bill at construction, bind the declared endpoint set, and carry a Peer through the handshake to an established Session. Slice 3.4 adds the data plane: each established Peer reassembles Messages in its own persistent receive buffer and delivers each whole one as a MessageReceived event copied into the shared frame arena. Retention, write batching and the Goodbye exchange are not yet built and land in the sub-issues that follow. Structs DiagnosticRecord A single diagnostic emitted to an IReactorDiagnostics Sink: a closed DiagnosticId, its fixed DiagnosticLevel, a tagged subject — none, Link, Source or Peer (ADR 0013) — and two numeric slots whose meaning is documented per DiagnosticId member. No strings, no object[], no closures — everything here lives on the stack and is built only after IsEnabled(DiagnosticLevel) passes. LinkCounters A point-in-time snapshot of one Link's counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from that Link's registration, with no reset, fetched by value and keyed by LinkId — there is no accessor that enumerates every Link's counters in one call. LinkId A Link's identity: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the slot is reused, so a stale LinkId held past a Link's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that slot (ADR 0014) rather than aliasing it. PeerCounters A point-in-time snapshot of one Peer's counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from that Peer's establishment, with no reset, fetched by value and keyed by PeerId — mirrors LinkCounters's Raw-profile shape and the same "no accessor enumerates every Peer's counters in one call" rule. PeerId A Peer's identity inside this process: the Reactor that issued it, a zero-based Slot index, and a generation counter that increments when the Slot is reused, so a stale PeerId held past a Peer's close compares unequal to whatever now occupies that Slot (ADR 0007) rather than aliasing it. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010), exactly as LinkId is the Raw profile's. RawEvent One event drained from a RawReactor. A ref struct because Payload aliases the frame arena directly and must never outlive the Frame it was drained in (ADR 0008). Kind determines exactly which other fields are populated — this slice implements DatagramReceived, Closed, Accepted, Connected, SegmentReceived, EndOfStream and Writable — the complete Raw profile roster. RawEventEnumerator The zero-allocation enumerator Drain() returns. A ref struct so that a foreach over it can yield RawEvent — itself a ref struct — without a heap-allocated IEnumerator<T>, following the same pattern as Span<T>'s own enumerator. ReactorCounters A point-in-time snapshot of the Reactor-scope counters (ADR 0013): monotonic figures running from construction, with no reset. Fetched by value so nothing lets a consumer hold a pointer into live state across a Pump; diffing two snapshots gives everything a reset would, from state the consumer already owns. Result The outcome of an operation whose failures are the caller's to check rather than the runtime's to throw — a wrong-kind call on a Link (Send on a datagram Link) or a send the remote end or the network refused. Error names the illegality or the platform failure in prose; there is no error code enumeration here because, unlike CloseReason, nothing about this failure needs to survive as permanent public API — a consumer branches on IsSuccess and logs or surfaces Error as-is. SendResult The outcome of one Send(LinkId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) call. Unlike Result, a stream send has a quantity worth reporting even on success: the Reactor holds no outbound bytes (ADR 0008), so Send takes what the socket will take right now and hands back the count — the caller keeps whatever was not taken, and BytesSent is how it learns how much that is. SessionEvent One event drained from a Session Reactor. A ref struct because Payload aliases the frame arena directly, and must never outlive the Frame it was drained in (ADR 0008). Kind determines exactly which other fields are populated. SessionEventEnumerator The zero-allocation enumerator every Session Reactor's Drain returns (ADR 0010), shared by both profiles via ReactorSockets.ISessionEventSource rather than duplicated per profile. A ref struct so that a foreach over it can yield SessionEvent — itself a ref struct — without a heap-allocated IEnumerator<T>, following the same pattern as Span<T>'s own enumerator. Source Who a datagram claims to be from — an unauthenticated hint about origin, never an identity (ADR 0014). Carried on the record path as a value type: { family, 16 address bytes, scope id, port }, roughly 56 bytes, so a Diagnostic or an Event never allocates to name a Source. Interfaces IReactorDiagnostics The Diagnostic Sink contract. Implementations are called synchronously, on the consumer's thread, inside Pump — a Sink that stalls stalls the Frame, and a Sink that throws is caught, counted as SinkFaulted, and disabled for the life of the Reactor (ADR 0005). Calling back into the Reactor from a Sink is a programmer error and throws. Enums CloseReason Why a Link closed, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration (ADR 0008): a consumer's permanent logic switches on this instead of a SocketError that differs between Windows and Unix. The exact SocketError travels in the DiagnosticRecord emitted at the same moment, linked to this only by the Link and the Pump it happened in. DiagnosticId A closed, permanent enumeration of diagnostic causes with explicit values in reserved blocks — common 1-99, Raw 100-199, datagram session 200-299, stream session 300-399 (ADR 0013) — so a future insertion cannot silently renumber an id a consumer has persisted. There is no None or Unknown member and zero is never used: every DiagnosticRecord has a cause by construction. DiagnosticLevel The minimum severity a IReactorDiagnostics Sink was installed to receive. Ordered by ascending severity so that a level is enabled when it is at least as severe as the installed MinimumLevel. DiagnosticSubjectKind Which field of a DiagnosticRecord's tagged subject is populated (ADR 0013). A record has exactly one subject, so a Sink or formatter switches on this rather than checking several optional fields for which one is set. DisconnectReason Why a Peer's Session ended, defined and kept stable by this library rather than borrowed from a platform enumeration. Deliberately not shared with the Raw profile's CloseReason (ADR 0008): most of the members a Session needs are protocol vocabulary Raw can never produce, and a single shared enumeration would leave one profile documenting members it cannot emit. RawEventKind Which kind of RawEvent a drained event is. This slice adds the stream-relevant kinds to the datagram-only roster shipped earlier (ADR 0008); Accepted lands with the listening-Link work, Connected with dialling, SegmentReceived and EndOfStream with stream reads, and Writable with partial sends. SendOutcome The outcome of one Send(PeerId, ReadOnlySpan<byte>) call. A bare enum rather than a result struct (unlike SendResult): a Session-level send has no partial-completion quantity worth reporting back — the framed Message either fit in the Peer's retention region whole, or it did not, so the outcome is the whole story. SessionEventKind Which kind of SessionEvent was drained, and therefore which of its fields carry meaning. Shared by both Session profiles (ADR 0010). SourceFamily The address family of a Source, carried as an explicit tag rather than inferred from the address bytes (ADR 0014). With DualMode never set, nothing in a 16-byte field distinguishes a zero-padded IPv4 address from an IPv6 one.
